sources.title: Slav and Semi-Slav search snippets (TheChessWorld, Chess Doctrine, Wikipedia Semi-Slav)

overview: Black supports d5 with ...c6 so that the centre is held by pawns while the light-squared bishop stays free to come out (usually to f5 or g4) before ...e6. The root is a crossroads: after 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 Black chooses the Pure Slav with ...dxc4 (active bishop, ...e5/...c5 breaks), the Semi-Slav with ...e6 (c6-d5-e6 triangle, theory-heavy and often sharp: Meran, Botvinnik, Anti-Meran), or the Chebanenko ...a6. White can also play the Exchange (cxd5 cxd5), a symmetrical structure with queenside minority attack ideas that has a drawish reputation, or quiet systems with 3.e3 or 3.Bf4. The Slav is played by many world champions (Botvinnik, Smyslov, Anand, Kramnik) and is regarded as sound; sources treat it as solid with room for counterplay rather than a forced-draw defence.

white_ideas.idea: Central expansion with e4 (after Nc3/e4 gambit-style ideas) and kingside pawn advances
Pressure on b7 and the queenside before Black plays ...dxc4 or ...a6

Exchange Slav: queenside expansion (source summary also mentions minority attacks; own understanding is that with both c-pawns gone the queenside is symmetrical, so a true minority attack is doubtful)
Quiet 3.e3 / 3.Bf4 development; aim to recover c4 with the bishop on c4

black_ideas.idea: Develop the light-squared bishop to f5 or g4 before ...e6
Pawn breaks ...e5 and ...c5 to free the position
Semi-Slav: build the c6-d5-e6 pawn triangle, later ...dxc4 and ...b5/...c5 queenside expansion
Hold the centre with pawns, equalise safely

typical_structures.structure: Symmetrical Exchange Slav structure (c-pawns exchanged, d4 against d5)
Pure Slav after ...dxc4: White centre pawns d4/e4 against Black's flexible c6/e-pawn breaks; open-ish
Semi-Slav c6-d5-e6 triangle; hanging pawns or open c-file after ...c5

character.notes: Wikipedia: balances solidity with dynamic counterplay, no forced early tactics. Chessable: solid yet dynamic rather than sterile. The Exchange Slav is drawish; the Semi-Slav branches (Meran, Botvinnik) are much sharper and theory-heavy. Main Pure Slav lines are solid with real tactics possible.

gambit.notes: After 3...dxc4 Black takes a pawn that White normally regains (Queen's Gambit style); not a gambit. Semi-Slav Botvinnik and Marshall lines have sacrifices in sublines.

soundness.notes: Fundamentally sound; played by Botvinnik, Smyslov, Anand and Kramnik (six games in the 2006 World Championship match).

structure.notes: Centre is held by pawns (c6/d5), tension at d5/c4; many lines keep central pawns on (Exchange, Semi-Slav triangle). Pure Slav after ...dxc4 allows e4 and an open game with ...e5 or ...c5 breaks. Pawn structure varies strongly by variation.

approach.notes: A defined reply to 1.d4 d5 2.c4, not a set-up played against anything. Mainstream at all levels including world-championship matches.

level.notes: Chessable says highly suitable for club players: reliability without excessive theory, understanding over memorisation. Wikipedia says it demands extensive theory in the main lines. Semi-Slav is theory-heavy; a snippet says beginners usually start with the Meran.

sublines_that_differ.name: Semi-Slav / Meran / Botvinnik
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 c6 3. Nf3 Nf6 4. Nc3 e6
sublines_that_differ.how: Theory-heavy, often very sharp; separate character (Botvinnik is an anchor for Sharp/Advanced).

sublines_that_differ.name: Exchange Slav
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 c6 3. cxd5 cxd5
sublines_that_differ.how: Symmetrical, solid and drawish; queenside minority attack ideas.

sublines_that_differ.name: Czech / Pure Slav
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 c6 3. Nf3 Nf6 4. Nc3 dxc4
sublines_that_differ.how: Open, active bishop, e4-e5 plans for White; more forcing than the Exchange.

sublines_that_differ.name: Chebanenko
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 c6 3. Nf3 Nf6 4. Nc3 a6

description.claim: The Slav is one of Black's most solid and reliable responses to the Queen's Gambit
description.note: Described as solid; sound at world-champion level. (2.c4 is the Queen's Gambit move order.)

description.claim: With ...c6 Black prepares to recapture on d5 with a pawn and keeps a robust central structure
The light-squared bishop is not locked in
description.note: Key difference from the QGD; but in the Semi-Slav ...e6 temporarily blocks it.

description.claim: Blend of solid defence and dynamic counter-attacking potential leading to structurally complex games
description.note: Wikipedia and Chessable both describe solid plus dynamic.

common_plans.claim: Black: Solidify the centre, develop the light-squared bishop (f5 or g4), prepare ...e5 or ...b5 to create counterplay
common_plans.note: Bishop to f5/g4, ...e5 and ...c5 breaks; ...b5 belongs to Meran/Semi-Slav and Pure Slav (after ...dxc4) lines.

common_plans.claim: White: control the centre, develop to pressure Black's set-up, and often launch a queenside minority attack (b4-b5) to create a weakness on c6
common_plans.note: Own understanding, flagged as such: in the Exchange Slav both c-pawns are traded, so there is no c6 pawn to target and no pawn-count minority; the article summary mentions minority attacks only in passing. In the main Slav White's plans are e4, pressure on b7 and development, not b4-b5.

common_plans.claim: Black: After cxd5 cxd5, equalise and use the solid structure to transition into a favourable endgame
common_plans.note: The Exchange Slav is described as drawish, with Black having little chance to win unless White is overambitious; Black aims for equality, not a favourable endgame.

common_plans.claim: White: In the Exchange Variation, play for a small but lasting space advantage and try to prove Black's set-up is passive
common_plans.note: Modern practice shows White can get legitimate edges with aggressive set-ups; the idea of a small edge is accurate.
